pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-mee-dah' — three even syllables, with the middle vowel bright and short.

kin.label: Chinese

pronunciation.note: Amida is Tier 2: the Japanese form loses the long ā and aspirated bh of the Sanskrit, so it preserves nothing ASCII cannot already write. The name's power is devotional, not orthographic.

domains.title: Buddha of Immeasurable Light
domains.subtitle: Pure Land, Faith, and the Promise of Rebirth
domains.lead: Amida is the Japanese face of Amitābha, the Buddha whose immeasurable light built a pure land in the west. For over a thousand years his name has been Japan's most repeated prayer — Namu Amida Butsu — and the promise behind it is radical: even those crushed by karma they cannot undo can be born in his Pure Land and attain enlightenment.

cards.name: Immeasurable Light
cards.desc: His name — Amida, from Sanskrit Amitābha — is itself the first teaching: light with no edge, dissolving the karma-darkness of beings.

cards.name: Pure Land (Sukhāvatī)
cards.desc: The Land of Bliss in the west: jeweled ponds and gold trees, where birth in a lotus guarantees the path to Buddhahood.

cards.name: Name as Vow
cards.desc: Hōnen (Senchakushū, 1198) and Shinran (Kyōgyōshinshō) taught that a single recitation, taken on faith, is the working of the vow itself.

cards.name: Welcoming Descent
cards.desc: Raigō painting: Amida descends on clouds with Kannon and Seishi — the deathbed vision of medieval Japan, from temple murals to death registers.

symbols.name: The Amida triad
symbols.meaning: Amida flanked by Kannon (Avalokiteśvara) and Seishi (Mahāsthāmaprāpta) — compassion and wisdom attending every descent

symbols.name: The nenbutsu rosary (juzu)
symbols.meaning: Beads counting Namu Amida Butsu; worn on the wrist of every Pure Land devotee since Hōnen's day

symbols.name: The western direction
symbols.meaning: He faces west — toward the setting sun and toward Sukhāvatī; the dying were laid with their heads west to meet his coming

symbols.name: The mudrā of welcome
symbols.meaning: The raised hand in raigō images, palm open — the gesture of one arriving to receive, not to judge

symbols.name: Halos of light
symbols.meaning: Radiant aureoles of immeasurable light — in Amida's case the body itself is the sermon

symbols.name: Lotus seat
symbols.meaning: Purity and transcendence; the faithful are reborn in Sukhāvatī's lotuses

mythology.lead: Amida's mythology runs from the Indian vows of Dharmākara through Chinese translation into Japan's nenbutsu movement: the radical teaching that calling the Buddha's name with faith is itself the path. His stories are devotional rather than epic — vows, recitations, and descents — and they reshaped how Japan faced death.

myths.title: The Forty-Eight Vows of Dharmākara
myths.text: In the Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra the Buddha tells how, in an inconceivably remote past, the monk Dharmākara knelt before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja and set himself a task no being had dared: to survey every Buddha-field in the ten directions, gather the best of each, and build from them a single land where no one who trusted him would fail to reach enlightenment. After five aeons of contemplation he pronounced forty-eight vows. The eighteenth — the Primal Vow (hongan) — promises that anyone who, with sincere entrusting, desires rebirth in his land and calls his name even ten times will be born there. Dharmākara then practiced for countless kalpas until the vows stood fulfilled, and he became Amida, whose Sukhāvatī lies to the west like a shore beyond every storm. The sūtra's logic is startling: enlightenment is not climbed but received, because someone else finished the climbing first.

myths.title: Hōnen Selects the Single Practice
myths.text: By the twelfth century the Tendai establishment taught that every practice could lead to awakening — and therefore, argued the monk Hōnen, none was being done wholeheartedly by ordinary people mired in the latter days of the Dharma. In 1198 he set down his answer in the Senchakushū: select the one practice the Buddha himself had promised would suffice — the nenbutsu, the calling of Amida's name, Namu Amida Butsu — and let every other good act adorn it rather than compete with it. His disciples carried the teaching from the capital to the fishing villages, until peasants and soldiers who had never read a sūtra were reciting the Buddha's name in fields and on battlefields. The authorities proscribed the movement in 1207 and exiled Hōnen, but the nenbutsu had already escaped every gate: the single practice made the highest path the commonest road.

myths.title: Shinran and the Tannishō
myths.text: Hōnen's disciple Shinran pushed the nenbutsu one step further — and into a new religion. If salvation depended on Amida's Primal Vow, then even the recitation must be the Buddha's own working through the believer; even faith was a gift, not an achievement. The saying attributed to him in the Tannishō became the movement's signature: even the good person attains birth in the Pure Land, how much more so the evil person — because the good still secretly trust their own goodness, while the evil have nothing left to trust but the vow. Driven from Kyoto and settled among the peasants of Kantō, Shinran married, raised a family, and wrote the Kyōgyōshinshō in huts and borrowed halls, founding what became Jōdo Shinshū, Japan's largest Buddhist school. The scandal of his teaching is its mercy: it works precisely for those the other paths screen out.

myths.title: Raigō and the Buddha Who Would Not Stay
myths.text: The myth Amida's devotees painted most is the raigō — the Welcoming Descent: on clouds, flanked by Kannon and Seishi, Amida comes down to meet the dying, and deathbed practice aimed every sense toward that arrival. Temple legends gave the descent a mischievous edge. Zenkōji's own tradition (Zenkōji engi) tells that when a summons came from the retired emperor in Kamakura, the temple's Amida image rose at night and set off eastward; the abbot Eikan chased it through the dark and caught hold of it, but the Buddha slipped from his arms — and only the head remained, the body going on to Kamakura, leaving Zenkōji the Eikanbetsu Amida, a face without a body eternally gazing east. A Buddha who refuses to stay put is the legend's whole point: Amida is bound to no temple, because his vow already covers every deathbed.

lore.syncretism: Amida is Japan's pronunciation of Amitābha, the Buddha venerated across Asia: Ēmítuó in China, Amit'a in Korea, A-di-đà in Vietnam. Japan's distinctive contribution was not a new doctrine but a new social reach — Hōnen and Shinran made the nenbutsu the practice of farmers, fishermen, warriors, and outcastes, so Amida became a household word rather than a monastic preserve. Japanese popular religion then braided him into older patterns: the warrior-kami Hachiman was declared a bodhisattva who protects devotees of the nenbutsu, medieval honji-suijaku thought read local deities as traces of Amida, and the dying were laid facing west — toward both the setting sun and the Pure Land. In China the complementary synthesis ran through the lay societies founded at Lushan in 402 CE, and in Tibet Amitābha presides over the red Buddha-family and the phowa practice that transfers consciousness to Sukhāvatī at death: one vow, received on three continents.
lore.culturalLegacy: Amida's name is among the most recited phrases in Japanese religious history; Namu Amida Butsu appears in literature and film as prayer, thanksgiving, and resigned acceptance alike. His architecture marks the country — Hōryūji, Byōdōin's Phoenix Hall on the ten-yen coin, Zenkōji with its never-displayed hidden image — and his images mark its deaths: raigō paintings and deathbed name-registers survive by the thousand. Jōdo and Jōdo Shinshū remain among Japan's largest Buddhist schools, and the nenbutsu still rings out each New Year. Restoring the name as Amida keeps the Japanese form — devotional, democratic, and distinctly un-Sanskrit — exactly as a thousand years of chanters pronounced it.
lore.extendedMeditation: Amida's teaching is a thought experiment carried out for a millennium: what if grace were real? What if the one thing required of you were simply to let yourself be saved? The Pure Land schools do not deny effort; they deny that effort is the currency of awakening. The nenbutsu is the sound of a person stopping the arithmetic — my merits, my failures, my progress — and entrusting the whole account to a vow made before this world existed. This is why the movement conquered Japan's margins first: fishermen, peasants, soldiers, the sick, who had no leisure for stages and contemplations. Amida is the patron of those too tired to climb. His light does not ask whether the one standing in it has earned the sun; it only asks that the eyes be open.
lore.archaeology: Byōdōin at Uji (1053 CE) is Japan's most famous Amida temple, its Phoenix Hall built as a built image of Sukhāvatī and its Amida by Jōchō setting the standard for Heian-period sculpture; both hall and image appear on the ten-yen coin. Chūsonji's Konjiki-dō — the gilded Hall of the Golden Hue at Hiraizumi (1124 CE) — stages the Pure Land in gold leaf and mother-of-pearl. Zenkōji in Nagano preserves the hidden Amida triad brought from the continent in the seventh century, and Kamakura's Great Buddha at Kōtoku-in (cast 1252, some eleven meters of bronze) gave Amida the open sea for a backdrop, while the Eikanbetsu tradition gives its face an eternal eastern gaze.
